title: Write a utility method `Function<T, R> unchecked(CheckedFunction<T, R> f)` that wraps a checked function into an unchecked one for use in streams.
shortTitle: Write a utility method Function<T, R> unchecked(CheckedFunction<T, R> f) to wrap a checked function for use in streams

s1_definition.profdef: You define a `CheckedFunction<T, R>` functional interface whose method declares `throws Exception`, and a generic static `unchecked` helper that adapts it to a standard `Function<T, R>` by catching any checked exception and rethrowing it as unchecked.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya builds a universal adapter: feed it any form that might throw a checked error, and it hands back a form the stream accepts, converting any error to an unchecked one.
s1_definition.oneliner: `unchecked(CheckedFunction)` adapts a checked-throwing lambda into a stream-compatible `Function`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You define a `CheckedFunction<T, R>` functional interface whose method declares `throws Exception`, and a generic static `unchecked` helper that adapts it to a standard `Function<T, R>` by catching any checked exception and rethrowing it as unchecked.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya builds a universal adapter: feed it any form that might throw a checked error, and it hands back a form the stream accepts, converting any error to an unchecked one.

**One line to remember:** `unchecked(CheckedFunction)` adapts a checked-throwing lambda into a stream-compatible `Function`.

sections.s2_technical:
First declare the interface: `@FunctionalInterface interface CheckedFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws Exception; }`. Then the generic helper `static <T, R> Function<T, R> unchecked(CheckedFunction<T, R> f)` returns a lambda `t -> { try { return f.apply(t); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } }`.

This gives you a single reusable adapter. Anywhere a stream needs a Function but your method throws a checked exception, you write `map(unchecked(this::risky))`. The generics keep it type-safe for any input and output types.

The senior nuance is that this centralises the checked-to-unchecked conversion so it is written once and reused, keeping every call site clean. I would make analogous wrappers for Consumer and Supplier, and I prefer wrapping in a specific unchecked type like UncheckedIOException over a bare RuntimeException where applicable, preserving the cause. For expected failures I still favour result-objects over exceptions, but this wrapper is the right tool when the method genuinely throws and the failure is exceptional.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Several pipelines at the National Bank of India call methods that throw checked exceptions, and the team wants one reusable adapter instead of repeating try-catch everywhere.

This is exactly what the unchecked wrapper does — it converts any checked function into a stream-ready Function once.

The code defines the `CheckedFunction interface and `StreamUtils.unchecked, plus a demo.

```
stream-utils/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/bank/streamutils/

```

javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/streamutils/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.streamutils.UncheckedDemo

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the strings "10", "20", "30".

Step 1: unchecked wraps the checked-throwing parseStrict method reference into an ordinary Function.

Step 2: map applies that Function to each string.

Step 3: Inside the wrapper, parseStrict runs in a try; for valid numbers it returns the int.

Step 4: The parsed integers are collected; a malformed value would be rethrown as an unchecked RuntimeException carrying the original cause.

```
INFO: parsed: [10, 20, 30]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CheckedFunction (throws Exception)
    │ unchecked(f)  →  Function (try f.apply catch → RuntimeException)
    ▼
  ["10","20","30"] → map(unchecked(parseStrict)) → [10, 20, 30]
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Reusable Checked→Unchecked Adapter ═══

  checked method → StreamUtils.unchecked(...) → stream-ready Function
     written once, reused across pipelines
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — unchecked wrapper utility ═══

  ┌─ centralised conversion ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CheckedFunction<T,R>: R apply(T) throws Exception           │
  │ unchecked(f): t -> try f.apply(t) catch → throw unchecked   │
  │ generic → type-safe for any T, R                           │
  │ one place to convert → clean call sites: map(unchecked(f))  │
  │ analogous wrappers for Consumer/Supplier; preserve cause    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   <<FunctionalInterface>>     │   │     StreamUtils      │
  │   CheckedFunction<T,R>        │◀──│ unchecked(CheckedFn) │
  │   + apply(T): R throws        │   │   → Function<T,R>    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. unchecked(this::risky) → Function
  2. map(that Function)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The utility has two parts. First I declare my own functional interface, CheckedFunction, whose single abstract method declares throws Exception, so a lambda or method reference that throws a checked exception can satisfy it. Then I write a generic static helper, unchecked, that takes a CheckedFunction and returns a standard Function by wrapping the call in a try-catch and rethrowing any checked exception as an unchecked RuntimeException, preserving the original cause.

With that in place, every stream call site stays clean — I just write map of unchecked of my risky method reference, and the conversion is handled behind the scenes. The generics keep it type-safe for any input and output types. At the National Bank of India this gave the team one reusable adapter instead of repeating the same try-catch in every pipeline.

The senior point I stress is centralising the checked-to-unchecked conversion so it is written once and applied everywhere, and making analogous wrappers for Consumer and Supplier so the whole stream toolkit is covered. I prefer rethrowing as a specific unchecked type like UncheckedIOException where it applies, always preserving the cause so the stack trace is intact. And I remember that for expected, recoverable failures I would still favour returning result-objects over throwing — this wrapper is for genuinely exceptional failures in methods that must declare a checked exception.

---

keyPoints: Checked exceptions in lambdas: compiler does not allow in map/filter
Wrap in try-catch inside the lambda, or create unchecked() wrapper utility
Collect both successes and errors: partition or custom collector
Design: keep lambdas simple, extract complex logic to named methods
